data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["A drug trial can randomize patients to placebo; a single panel evaluation cannot randomly assign panelists to a 'placebo checklist' without a separate experimental condition.","Drug effect sizes are typically continuous; checklist compliance may be binary or thresholded, changing the statistical structure.","The placebo effect in drugs is a psychological response; the 'compliance effect' here is a procedural artifact, not a psychological treatment effect."],"overturn_conditions":["If a placebo checklist yields the same accuracy as the valid checklist, the original gain is compliance, not discrimination.","If the outcome is not truly objective, the regression test conflates judge agreement with accuracy."],"shared_structure":["In drug trials, a placebo control isolates specific pharmacological efficacy from non-specific compliance effects; here, a validity-decomposition isolates specific cue-discrimination from non-specific checklist-following.","Both require a counterfactual arm: the placebo arm / the base-rate-only checklist arm.","The outcome is objectively measurable in both, allowing a clean efficacy signal."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SCR_001","SRC_006"],"transfer_claims":["The logic of the placebo-controlled trial transfers to checklist evaluation: one needs a 'placebo checklist' (high in compliance-cues, low in task-validity) to establish that the original checklist's gain is not mere compliance.","The concept of 'specific efficacy' vs. 'non-specific effects' transfers: a checklist can have high face-validity (compliance) without high criterion-validity (discrimination).","The requirement for a pre-specified primary outcome transfers: if the checklist's gain is only visible on post-hoc subscales, it is likely a compliance artifact."]},"claim":"The panel's apparent superiority is genuine only if individual checklist items possess non-trivial, independently measurable criterion validity. Within a single evaluation, one can distinguish genuine discrimination from mere compliance by examining whether the panel's per-item scores carry information about the outcome beyond what a fixed base-rate rule predicts: if residuals of per-item scores against the outcome are uninformative, the panel is merely complying with a surface procedure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the outcome is highly skewed and the checklist merely encodes the base-rate, the incremental validity test will show zero contribution from individual items, revealing the gain as compliance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the evaluation set has low outcome variance, the regression lacks power and the test is inconclusive, not confirming genuine gain.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the panel's per-item scores are perfectly collinear, one cannot isolate item-level validity from a single evaluation, and the test fails to distinguish.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Each checklist item is a noisy classifier. Genuine reliability gain requires that the ensemble of items be collectively more informative than any single heuristic. If the checklist is valid, item-level scores will show a gradient: cases that the panel scores high on the relevant cues will have systematically higher probability of the target outcome. If the gain is mere compliance, item scores will be internally consistent (panelists agree) but the mapping from item-scores to outcome will be flat or entirely mediated by a single base-rate proxy. A single evaluation can estimate this by regressing the outcome on the panel's per-item scores and testing whether the incremental variance explained by non-base-rate items is significant.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
